rv.q: Skeleton Crew does all that and more, finding hope in the unlikeliest of places, like a cluttered, ramshackle break room of a noisy, about-to-fail factory in an about-to-fail city like Detroit.
Morisseau gives you meat along with dem bones.

Morisseau understands, and in this finely wrought monologue conveys concisely, that blue-collar work can be as rewarding, and inspiring of loyalty and pride, as better-paying, more prestigious and less physically demanding jobs.
Morisseau has penned a true ensemble piece highlighted by individuals who are flawed, relatable and vastly human.
The production benefits enormously from a cast that breathes authentic life into Wilson's characters.

It's that pride that Morisseau wants to pay tribute to, and in a play that might have nothing but bad awaiting its characters as the huge thumb of capitalism hovers over their heads, we're left with a little bit of hope.
In the drafty hall, Morisseau’s carefully banked fires start to flicker.
She knows how to get my motor running.
Morisseau’s dad was right: She knew what she was doing, and definitely got somewhere good.
This is theatre that reminds you why theater is the closest thing to hallowed ground we have.
Morriseau has created a brilliant, modern workplace tragedy, masterfully attuned to the ways the American Dream has made sleepwalkers of us all.
Rashad is fantastic as the 'tough as bricks' Faye, and Dirden is simply spectacular as the buttoned-up Reggie.
Morisseau’s well-built and affecting play gives us a strikingly relevant portrait of an oppressive economy and those struggling to find their way through it.

cn.t: Morisseau's compassionate drama about Detroit auto workers earns praise for its lyrical writing and stellar performances, particularly Phylicia Rashad's, though some critics find it stronger on atmosphere than dramatic tension.

sg.ra: SeatPlan notes rows A-D are ideal at this 634-seat house: close enough to catch facial expressions but not neck-craning. Row AA also called out for superior legroom. No overhang concerns (Mezzanine overhang starts at row G per SeatPlan).

Headout and SeatPlan both flag rows E-J as the best price-to-sightline ratio: meaningfully cheaper than the A-D premium band while staying close in a 634-seat room. Slight orchestra rake keeps sightlines clean. Mezzanine overhang (per SeatPlan) begins at row G but the intimate room means no sound-deadening issue in this band.

sg.vl: Under the overhang but still engaged
sg.ra: SeatPlan confirms the Mezzanine overhangs from row G back, so K-Q sit fully under. The room is small enough (Headout: 'one of Broadway's more intimate spaces') that rear orchestra remains engaged. Rows P and Q are accessibility-friendly (no aisle stairs per folliesbroadway). Legroom tightens beyond row O per SeatPlan.

Headout and SeatPlan both name AA-BB center as premier seats with 'clean, direct look at the stage' and elevation that improves the view. aviewfrommyseat user on Mezzanine L row A aisle reported 'lots of legroom' with only a thin safety bar as minor issue. Excellent rake across the mezzanine.

SeatPlan and Headout both emphasize that the mezzanine has 'excellent rake' keeping all rows elevated with clean sightlines; Headout says 'no truly bad seat in the house'.
